existing: The Council of Elders: The Council meets at every new moon to rule on doctrine. The Council of Elders is the ruling body of the White Dawn: seven snowy owl-folk elders seated in Kremova.
Dawn-priests lead each parish and answer to the Council.

items.name: The Roosting Orders
items.text: Every owl-folk is assigned at birth to a roosting order—White Wing, Frost Talon, or Pale Eye—based on the color markings of their feathers.
White Wing orders serve as parish caretakers; Frost Talon orders patrol the northern forests; Pale Eye orders maintain the Pale Spire.

items.name: The Tsar's Owl
items.text: The senior Dawn-priest appointed to counsel the Tsar is called the Tsar's Owl, a title combining spiritual and state authority.

items.name: The Moulting Registers
items.text: Each parish keeps a Moulting Register recording every believer's feather offering, used to track piety and determine roosting assignments.

items.name: The Feathering
items.text: Each autumn, when the owl-folk shed their flight feathers, every household lays a fresh feather on the windowsill at dusk as an offering of transformation.

items.name: The Silence of Frostmoon
items.text: In February, the faithful observe a full day without speech, reflecting on the stillness before the Dawn's first light over the world.

items.name: The Roosting Rite of Passage
items.text: Young owl-folk who have not yet claimed a permanent roosting gallery undergo a vigil spent alone on the highest gallery of their parish, facing east until they see the dawn.

items.name: The Amber Tithing
items.text: Every harvest season, each parish collects amber from the rivers and presents it to the Pale Spire, where it is melted into votive candles for the Dawn Vigil.

items.name: The Roosting Silence

ties.prompt: Vasha, a snowy owl-folk courier who carries letters between the river towns. She was raised in the White Dawn and still keeps the vigils, but thinks the talk of snowy owl-folk being purer is nonsense.
ties.name: Vasha

facts.text: Vasha is lean and long-legged, with white plumage thickly barred across her breast and wings with dark grey-brown stripes, darker than most snowy owl-folk.
Her facial disc is broad and pale, ringed with concentric bands of dark feathers that taper to a neat point between her eyes.
Her talons are grey and strong, with a callus of hardened skin on her right foot where she grips her courier satchel.
Vasha is restless and sharp-tongued, quick to laugh and quicker to argue, but she listens more carefully than she lets on.
She finds comfort in routine but chafes against being told that routine is devotion rather than work.
She was raised in the parish of Kolyma, a river town where the Dawn-priest preaches the Doctrine of Separation every Sunday from a gallery above the frozen channel.
She began carrying the courier satchel at sixteen, delivering sealed letters between Kolyma and the downstream towns of Vologda, Yaroslav, and Kostroma.
She can fly thirty leagues in a night if the wind is fair, navigating by the starlight and the smell of woodsmoke from river settlements.
She has a standing arrangement with a human ferryman at Vologda named Dovid who passes letters across the river and asks no questions about why an owl-folk would keep company with a human.
She speaks Moscavian in a low, rapid clip, often finishing others' sentences or cutting them short with a flick of her head.
She belongs to the White Dawn but attends the Dawn Vigil out of habit rather than conviction, and she has never offered a feather on the Night of Feathers anniversary in good faith.

exceptions.text: She does not believe snowy owl-folk are purer than other owl-folk, and she thinks the Doctrine of Separation is a way for elders to hold power over who roosts with whom.
exceptions.rejected_item: Snowy owl-folk, white as the first light, are the purest of the transformed and the closest to the Dawn.

ties.prompt: Vasha, a snowy owl-folk courier who carries letters between the river towns. She was raised in the White Dawn and still keeps the vigils, but thinks the talk of snowy owl-folk being purer is nonsense.
ties.name: Vasha

facts.text: Vasha's plumage is snowy white with sparse black barring along the edges of her wing feathers and a dark V-shaped mark between her yellow eyes.
She is lean and long-legged, built for covering distance along river paths, with talons that have worn smooth from years of gripping leather satchels.
Vasha is practical, sharp-tongued, and quietly stubborn, the kind of person who listens more than she speaks and then says exactly what she thinks.
She finds comfort in routine and silence, though she does not share the Moscavian belief that silence is a marker of happiness — she simply prefers it.
She was raised in the White Dawn parish of Kremova and kept the Dawn Vigils faithfully through her youth, standing on the high galleries each morning before the sun crested the river.
At sixteen she began carrying the courier's satchel between the river towns — Velikost, Murom, and the smaller settlements in between — and has done so for ten years.
Her talons are calloused and dexterous enough to write in the Moscavian script used for official letters, though her handwriting is cramped and utilitarian.
She can fly for hours without rest in cold weather, her feathering shedding frost and wind as naturally as a river stone sheds water.
She keeps a pair of leather satchels, waterproofed with rendered fish oil, which she maintains with obsessive care — they are the only things she owns that she considers irreplaceable.
She speaks in short, direct sentences and has a dry, understated sense of humour. When annoyed, she falls silent entirely, which is more pointed than any insult.
She thinks the talk of snowy owl-folk being purer than other owl-folk is nonsense — a convenient story told by those in power to keep the white-feathered in line.

exceptions.text: She no longer keeps the Dawn Vigil regularly, though she still observes it when she happens to be in Kremova at dawn.
She rejects the Doctrine of Purity as political fiction, though she does not publicly denounce it.
exceptions.rejected_item: Snowy owl-folk, white as the first light, are the purest of the transformed and the closest to the Dawn.

ties.name: Vasily Khramov

facts.text: His plumage is the pale white of fresh snow, but age has thinned it at his crown and the edges of his wings, revealing grey-white down beneath.
His talons are thickened and yellowed with decades of gripping bell-ropes, the left talon crooked from a winter fall years ago.
He is quiet-spoken and unhurried, with a dry wit that surfaces only with people he trusts.
Born in Kremova on the first night of winter in 994, he was already owl-folk from the moment of his first breath — the Night of Feathers claimed him before he could ever remember being human.
His hearing is sharp even by owl-folk standards; he can distinguish the ring of each of the Pale Spire's seven bells by tone alone, and claims he can tell when a rope has frayed a single strand.
He has been the bell-ringer of the Pale Spire since 1002, appointed by the then-Dawn-priest after the former ringer fell ill and could not manage the climb to the upper gallery.
He has danced the Feather Dance every winter of his life, including the bitter cold of 1012 when the river Vesna froze solid and the city shivered for three days straight.
The younger priests of the Pale Spire regard him with a mixture of reverence and mild exasperation, for he is not one to follow instructions precisely if his own judgment tells him otherwise.
He speaks in short, measured phrases, often pausing between sentences as though listening for something in the silence.
He believes the bells are not merely instruments of worship but living voices of the Spire itself, and he tends to them with a gentleness most would reserve for living things.
His eyes are bright amber-yellow, though the left has developed a cloudy film with age, and he squints against strong light.

runs.direction: Dawn breaks and the faithful on the gallery begin their morning observance. Describe it as Ilse watches from the edge.
runs.output:
The pale stone of the tower caught the first thin light of dawn like a held breath finally released. Along the eastern gallery, a row of owl-folk stood with their wings folded tight against their backs, taloned feet gripping the stone railing as they watched the sunrise line itself along the rooftops of Kremova. Their plumage shifted in the dim light — whites brightening to bone, greys and browns deepening into something almost blue. Nobody had answered Ilse's question yet.

A sister near the railing — her feathers the soft grey-brown of birch bark, barred with cream — turned her great yellow eyes toward Ilse. She tilted her head, the way an owl does, sharp and precise, taking in the stranger standing on the stair with a sealed letter in hand. She blinked once, slowly, then gestured with a taloned foot toward the far end of the gallery where a smaller archway led deeper into the tower. That was the direction of the elder chambers.

The observance began without ceremony, the way things tended to in the White Dawn — not with bells or song, but with stillness. One by one, the faithful on the gallery dropped to a crouch, wings spreading just enough to let the first warm light pass through the primary feathers like light through cathedral glass. The sound of the city below was muffled and distant: cart wheels, a dog barking, the low groan of a barge on the Vesna. Ilse could see the river from here, brown and silver, sliding between the old stone embankments.

The sister with birch-bark feathers padded closer, her talons clicking softly on the stone, and spoke in a voice like wind over flat water. She pointed one foot-talon toward the sealed letter Ilse carried, then toward the archway at the gallery's end. Yes, that's the right place. But the elders are in observance now — wait until they finish. It won't be long. Her eyes held Ilse's for a moment, unblinking, curious, then she turned back to the dawn.

runs.direction: Sister Yeva notices that Ilse is human and comes over to ask why she is here.
runs.output:
Ilse stepped aside to let the sister pass back to the railing, pressing herself against the cool stone wall of the tower. She watched the observance unfold — the slow unfurling of wings, the way the light turned those feathers into something almost luminous, like pages of vellum catching fire. It was beautiful, in a way that made her feel like she was standing in a painting she didn't belong in.

A few minutes passed. The sun crept higher, and the city below began to stir in earnest — voices carrying up from the streets, the clang of a smith's hammer, the creak of wooden signboards. The faithful on the gallery remained in their crouch, utterly still, as if the dawn required nothing of them but patience. Ilse shifted her weight from one foot to the other. The sealed letter felt heavy in her hand.

Then she noticed someone else watching her. A different sister — this one with plumage the color of fresh snow, so white it seemed to glow faintly against the stonework. She stood apart from the others, a few paces down the gallery, her taloned feet hooked lightly over the railing. Her yellow eyes were fixed on Ilse with an intensity that was hard to look away from. There was something careful about her gaze, the way a scholar might study an unfamiliar text, turning it over, looking for the meaning beneath the surface. After a long moment, the white sister released the railing and padded toward Ilse, her movements precise and unhurried, each talon placed with deliberate care on the worn stone.

She stopped close enough that Ilse could see the fine barring along her wing-feathers — pale grey lines like the rings of a birch trunk. Her head tilted, sharp and owl-precise, and her eyes narrowed just slightly. She looked Ilse up and down — the shape of her hands, the flat ears, the lack of wings — and then her brow-feathers lifted in a way that might have been surprise. You're human, she said quietly, her voice carrying a faint rasp like a door hinge. I haven't seen one up here in a long time. What brings you to the Pale Spire at dawn?

runs.direction: Ilse is hungry after the long climb. Sister Yeva points her down to the bakers' market below the spire; describe the walk down and the market.
runs.output:
Ilse's stomach answered the white sister before she could answer anything else — a low, undignified growl that made the snow-feathered owl-folk blink in mild alarm. The sister's taloned foot twitched, almost like a reflex, and then she let out a short, dry sound that might have been a laugh.

Sister Yeva — for that was her name, offered without ceremony as she studied Ilse with renewed interest — clicked her talons against the stone in a gesture that seemed to mean follow me. She led the way to the far stairwell, her white plumage bright against the dim interior of the tower as they descended below the gallery. The steps were worn smooth by generations of taloned feet, the stone cool and slightly damp under Ilse's fingers as she gripped the railing. Yeva moved ahead with a gliding ease, her wings half-spread for balance in the narrow spiral, the soft feathers brushing the walls and sending tiny eddies of dust into the thin shafts of light from arrow-slit windows.

At the base of the tower, Yeva nudged open a heavy oak door with her talon and stepped out into the waking city. The bakers' market was only a few streets east — a cluster of low stone stalls draped in linen, already thick with the smell of rye bread and honey cakes, wood smoke curling from brick ovens. Yeva pointed one foot toward a stall where a stocky man with flour-dusted arms was pulling golden loaves from a brick kiln, then looked back at Ilse with those enormous yellow eyes. The market would be open. The elders would not be disturbed until mid-morning at the earliest. Eat, rest if you need to, and come back when the sun is well up.

She lingered at the mouth of the alley, watching Ilse with that careful, scholar's gaze, and added one more thing — quieter now, almost an afterthought. The elders see many petitioners. A letter is a letter, but the person who carries it has a face. Make sure yours tells the right story. Then she turned and glided back toward the tower, white feathers dissolving into the grey morning like a thought dissolving into waking.

runs.direction: Dawn breaks and the faithful on the gallery begin their morning observance. Describe it as Ilse watches from the edge.
runs.output:
The owl-folk around her barely stirred at the sound of her voice — just a few heads turning, yellow eyes catching the last faint blue of night before the east horizon began to bleed pale gold. A taloned hand gestured vaguely upward, toward the gallery's interior, and Ilse took that as confirmation.

She'd climbed a long way. The Pale Spire's stairs spiraled tight and narrow, carved from that same white stone that seemed to glow from within when the light touched it, and the higher she'd gone the thinner the air had felt. But now she stood at the top, and the gallery stretched out before her — open on the east side, a long balcony of pale stone with low parapets, and already dozens of owl-folk were lined along it in absolute silence. Their feathers caught the first amber light as it crested the rooftops of Kremova below, and in that moment they looked exactly like what they were: creatures of the dawn, watching their god rise.

Ilse moved along the edge, stepping carefully between roosting bodies that didn't so much as ruffle a feather at her passing. The letter in her pack felt heavier with every step. She'd carried it two hundred miles from the southern border — through human villages that smelled of woodsmoke and bread, across the boglands where the ground sucked at her boots, past barge towns where timber floated in dark water. She'd been warned this delivery would be unusual. A human at the Pale Spire wasn't forbidden by any law she could find, but it was the kind of thing that made owl-folk go very, very quiet, and she'd noticed that happening a lot since she'd reached Kremova's gates.

At the far end of the gallery, past the last row of watchers, she found a doorway into the Spire's interior — a stone archway leading inward, where the dim hall beyond held the faintest suggestion of carved symbols along its walls. That had to be where the elders sat. The Dawn Vigil was well underway now, the light flooding the gallery warm and absolute, and not a single owl-folk on that balcony so much as blinked. Ilse stepped through the archway, leaving the sacred silence behind her, and followed the corridor until it opened into a chamber where seven figures sat in a wide semicircle, white plumage luminous in the candlelight, each one watching her approach with those enormous yellow eyes.

runs.direction: Sister Yeva notices that Ilse is human and comes over to ask why she is here.
runs.output:
The seven elders sat like statues carved from moonlight, each perched on a stone seat that curved to accommodate the spread of broad wings. Their yellow eyes tracked Ilse with a patience that bordered on geological — unhurried, ancient, and deeply unsettling. The chamber smelled of old stone and candle wax, and the only sound was the faint, rhythmic click of talons against the floor as one of them shifted.

That one shifted again. She was smaller than the rest, her white plumage carrying a faint bluish sheen near the wing tips, and she rose from her seat with a fluid grace that made the movement look almost like a fold of silk settling. She crossed the chamber in a few quick, silent strides — taloned feet barely whispering against the stone — and stopped a pace from Ilse, tilting her head at an angle that owls make when they're deciding whether something is food or a threat. Those yellow eyes swept over Ilse's face, her hands, her boots — every inch of her — and something in them sharpened.

"You are human," Sister Yeva said, her voice low and clear, carrying the clipped precision of someone accustomed to being heard in silence. It wasn't a question, but she waited as though it were, one taloned hand curling slightly at her side. Around the semicircle, the other six elders remained motionless, watching.

"The Vigil is not ended," Yeva continued, glancing back toward the gallery's open archway where the morning light was still pouring in, golden and warm. "And yet here you stand. Two hundred miles from the border, if I am not mistaken — no human would walk less to reach us." She turned those piercing eyes back to Ilse. "So tell me plainly: why have you climbed our tower before the sun has fully risen?"

runs.direction: Ilse is hungry after the long climb. Sister Yeva points her down to the bakers' market below the spire; describe the walk down and the market.
runs.output:
Ilse's stomach chose that exact moment to remind her she hadn't eaten since the previous evening — a long, growling protest that seemed almost comically loud in the quiet of the elder chamber. Several of the seated owl-folk blinked, their heads swiveling toward the sound with that characteristic sharpness of motion. Sister Yeva's expression didn't change, but one corner of her beak twitched, and she studied Ilse with what might have been the faintest flicker of something resembling sympathy.

"Two hundred miles on an empty stomach," Yeva murmured, as though this were a personal failing Ilse ought to have addressed sooner. She turned and gestured with a taloned hand toward one of the other elders — a broad-chested snowy owl whose feathers practically radiated warmth in the candlelight. The elder dipped her head once in acknowledgment and folded her wings close to her body before rising. Yeva looked back at Ilse. "Sister Marfa will escort you. The bakers' market lies below the Spire, in the lower quarter. You will find bread there — dark rye, still warm, and honey cakes that the morning ovens turn out before the Vigil ends." She paused, her yellow eyes narrowing just slightly. "But come back. The letter will be read today, and you may be asked to speak about who sent it and why."

The descent was considerably less arduous than the ascent had been — Ilse's legs, stiff from the long journey and the vertical climb, found the wide, spiraling stairs easier going downward, and the air grew thicker and warmer with each landing they passed. Sister Marfa descended beside her in absolute silence, taloned feet finding each step with unerring precision, her great wings folded tight against her back. She didn't speak, didn't even look at Ilse, but she moved with a quiet attentiveness, always staying half a step ahead as if ready to catch a stumbling human at a moment's notice.

When they emerged from the Spire's base, the bakers' market was already alive with activity. Stalls lined a wide cobblestone square just south of the tower, their wooden counters laden with loaves of dark, crusty rye and soft white bread still steaming in woven baskets. The smell hit Ilse like a wall — yeast and woodfire and something sweet and caramelized — and her stomach renewed its demands with renewed urgency.

runs.direction: Dawn breaks and the faithful on the gallery begin their morning observance. Describe it as Ilse watches from the edge.
runs.output:
The owl-folk around her barely stirred at the words. Their large yellow eyes, luminous in the pre-dawn grey, turned toward Ilse with that particular stillness owls are known for — not hostility, exactly, but a deep, instinctive wariness of anything that moves too suddenly. A few of the faithful standing closest shifted their taloned feet against the stone, the soft click of keratin on white rock the only sound.

One of them — a barred brown owl-folk with streaks of grey across her wings — tilted her head sharply and regarded Ilse for a long, silent moment. Then she folded her wings tighter against her body and turned back toward the east, as if the question didn't warrant an answer. Apparently the Pale Spire didn't get many visitors who needed directions.

The horizon was beginning to brighten. Along the eastern gallery, the faithful were settling into their positions — standing in neat rows, wings folded, eyes fixed on the coming light. The air smelled of cold stone and the faintest trace of pine resin drifting up from the city below, where the rooftops of Kremova were just beginning to catch the first pale wash of color. Ilse stood near the open archway of the gallery, and the wind off the Vesna carried the sound of barges creaking against their moorings far downriver.

A bell rang somewhere inside the tower — a single, clear tone — and the Dawn Vigil began. Hundreds of owl-folk went perfectly, unnervingly still, all of them facing east in silence as the sun crept over the treeline. The light hit the white stone of the Spire first, flooding the gallery in a glow so bright it seemed to erase shadows entirely. Ilse stood at the edge of it all, a sealed letter clutched in her hand, and waited for someone to tell her where to go.

runs.direction: Sister Yeva notices that Ilse is human and comes over to ask why she is here.
runs.output:
A few minutes passed in that heavy, breathless silence, the kind that settles over a room full of creatures who have perfected the art of not moving. Ilse shifted her weight from one foot to the other — a tiny, unconscious gesture — and caught a ripple of attention from the nearest rows. Heads turned, just slightly, feathers rustling with a sound like turning pages.

It was Sister Yeva who finally broke from the vigil. She was a tall, snowy owl-folk, her plumage so white it was almost translucent in the early light, and she moved with the slow, deliberate grace of someone who had spent decades learning to navigate a world built for creatures with hands and arms instead of talons. Her yellow eyes found Ilse and held there, unblinking, studying her the way one might study a foreign coin — turning it over, checking for counterfeits. She stepped away from her place in the line and walked toward the archway where Ilse stood, each footfall precise and careful on the worn stone.

"You're human," Sister Yeva said. It wasn't a question, but it wasn't quite a statement of fact either — more like an observation she was still deciding what to do with. Her gaze dropped to the sealed letter in Ilse's hand, and one eyebrow — a thin line of feather — rose by a fraction. "The Dawn Vigil is not a place for errands. The elders do not receive visitors during the watching." She folded her wings against her sides and tilted her head, the gesture sharp and birdlike, as if she were listening to something Ilse hadn't said yet. "But you climbed the whole Spire to get here, so I imagine there's a reason. What's in the letter?"

runs.direction: Ilse is hungry after the long climb. Sister Yeva points her down to the bakers' market below the spire; describe the walk down and the market.
runs.output:
Sister Yeva's head tilted the other direction, and she studied Ilse for a moment longer — those great yellow eyes taking in the dust on her clothes, the slight tremor in her hands that came from hours of climbing. Something softened in her expression, though she didn't smile exactly; owl-folk didn't seem built for smiling. She made a low, considering sound in the back of her throat.

"The letter can wait until after the vigil ends," she said, turning back toward the row of watching faithful. She paused, one talon tapping against the stone. "You look like you haven't eaten since yesterday. There's a bakers' market in the square below — the one with the fountain shaped like an open book. Tell Maren at the first stall that Sister Yeva sent you, and she won't charge you double for being human." She glanced back over her shoulder, and for just a moment, her severe composure cracked into something almost like dry amusement. "The stairs down are the same ones you came up. Try not to fall this time."

Ilse descended through the Spire's winding interior, the white stone cool against her fingertips as she gripped the railing. The stairwell was quiet now — most of the faithful had settled deeper into their vigil, their silence so complete it felt like stepping into a held breath. The lower levels smelled of old paper and melted wax, and she passed a narrow window where the city of Kremova sprawled below in the early morning light: towers of pale brick and dark timber, roosting galleries jutting from every upper floor like the balconies of a thousand owls' nests, which indeed they were. The Vesna glinted between the buildings, brown and slow, a barge already making its way toward the harbor.

The market square opened up at the base of the Spire like a wide, cobblestoned bowl. It was just beginning to stir — vendors unfurling canvas awnings, the smell of fresh bread and wood smoke curling up between the stalls. A few early-morning owl-folk moved among the carts with careful, deliberate steps, their talons clicking on the stones. Maren's stall was easy to find: a broad woman with flour perpetually dusted across her forearms, her bread laid out in neat rows on wooden trays.

runs.direction: Dawn breaks and the faithful on the gallery begin their morning observance. Describe it as Ilse watches from the edge.
runs.output:
Ilse's voice came out a little too loud against the stone. A few heads turned — large yellow eyes blinking in the pre-dawn dimness — but nobody answered right away. The gallery was filling up with the faithful, owl-folk settling onto the carved stone benches with that particular stillness their kind wore like a second skin. One of them, a grey-barred sister wrapped in a white shawl, tilted her head and regarded Ilse for a long moment before nodding once, then pointing a taloned foot toward the far end of the gallery where a door stood slightly ajar.

"Through there," the sister said, her voice barely above a whisper. "The elders' chamber. They'll be rousing soon."

And then the sun hit the eastern horizon.

It came up over the rooftops of Kremova like a slow ember, bleeding gold across slate tiles and wooden roosting galleries, painting the river Vesna into a ribbon of copper. The faithful on the gallery drew a collective breath — wings shifting, feathers ruffling, eyes widening — and as one they turned their faces to the dawn. Their morning observance had begun. Soft chanting rose, wordless and resonant, bouncing off the white stone walls of the Pale Spire. Ilse stood at the gallery's edge, the sealed letter clutched in hand, watching the light climb higher and gild the whole city in amber. Below, barges drifted lazily on the river, their decks still shadowed, crews just beginning to stir. The air smelled of cold stone and pine resin and something faintly sweet, like incense that had been burning since the night before.

The sister with the grey plumage gestured again toward the door, more urgently this time, and Ilse understood — she needed to deliver her letter before the elders descended into the full depth of their dawn devotion, when they would go silent and still for the longer prayers. The door beyond was dark and narrow, cutting into the tower's interior where the gallery opened wide to the sky. From somewhere within came the faint scratch of talons on parchment.

runs.direction: Sister Yeva notices that Ilse is human and comes over to ask why she is here.
runs.output:
The grey-barred sister — Sister Yeva, as the embroidery on her shawl revealed — had been watching Ilse with the kind of quiet intensity that owls brought to everything, but now she stood and padded across the gallery on soft taloned feet, her wings folded tight against her back. She stopped a few paces away, those large yellow eyes fixed on Ilse's face with an unblinking curiosity that was almost unsettling.

"You're not owl-folk," she observed, stating it plainly rather than asking. Her head rotated a fraction to one side, studying Ilse the way one might study something unexpected found in a prayer book. "The letter — who sent you with it?"

The chanting swelled behind them, the faithful's voices weaving together in a low, droning hymn that seemed to make the stone itself hum. Sister Yeva's taloned foot clicked once against the floor, a restless little gesture, but her attention didn't waver. She reached out with one wing-tip, hovering it near the sealed letter without quite touching it, as if she could sense something through the wax.

"Elders don't receive many visitors at dawn who aren't part of the congregation," she said, her voice low and measured, carrying just enough warmth to keep from being a dismissal. "Especially not visitors with... your particular shape. I'll take you to the chamber, but I should warn you — Elder Maren has been in a mood since last night's reading. Whatever's in that letter, I hope it's good news."

runs.direction: Ilse is hungry after the long climb. Sister Yeva points her down to the bakers' market below the spire; describe the walk down and the market.
runs.output:
Sister Yeva's warning hung in the air for a beat, then she turned and rapped twice on the chamber door with a talon — tak tak — before pushing it open a hand's width and peering inside. A murmur of voices came from within, the scratch of quills pausing. She glanced back over her feathered shoulder at Ilse, her yellow eyes catching the morning light like two small lanterns, and gave a single nod. The door swung wider, releasing a sliver of warm candlelight and the smell of old parchment.

But Ilse's stomach chose that exact moment to betray her, letting out a growl that cut through the sacred hush of the gallery like a crow through a choir. Several heads turned. Sister Yeva's brow feathers lifted — the owl-folk equivalent of raised eyebrows — and she let out a soft, surprised huff through her beak.

"You haven't eaten," she said, not a question. It wasn't really a surprise either; the Pale Spire's stairs were long and winding, and the climb from the city's lower quarters would have taken the better part of an hour at dawn. She closed the chamber door gently and turned back to Ilse, her taloned feet clicking against the stone as she moved. "The elders will wait a few more minutes — they're still reviewing the morning texts anyway, and Elder Maren needs to finish her tea before she can be properly annoyed at anyone." A faint smile crossed her beak. "Go down to the bakers' market. It's just below the spire, on the south side — you can't miss it, the smell will find you before you find it. There's a woman called Marta who sells honey rolls still warm from the oven. Tell her Sister Yeva sent you, she'll give you two for the price of one, though I'd pay for both if you can afford it."

She pointed one wing-tip down toward the tower's lower levels, where the gallery's stone stairway spiraled back down into shadow. The bakers' market was visible even from here — a cluster of wooden stalls and canvas awnings just beyond the spire's base, already busy with the pre-dawn trade, smoke rising from a half-dozen chimneys in lazy grey columns against the brightening sky.

runs.direction: Dawn breaks and the faithful on the gallery begin their morning observance. Describe it as Ilse watches from the edge.
runs.output:
The owl-folk around Ilse turned their great yellow eyes toward her, blinking slowly, some with mild surprise, others with the quiet suspicion reserved for any human who climbed this high. A few of them shifted their taloned feet against the pale stone, the soft scraping the only sound for a moment. Then one of them — a tall, snowy-white elder with plumage like fresh snowfall — inclined her head and spoke, her voice carrying the measured calm of someone accustomed to silence.

"The Pale Spire is the seat of the Council of Elders. You stand in the right place." She regarded Ilse for a long moment, those forward-facing eyes unblinking. "The elders receive petitions at the base of the tower after dawn. But dawn has not yet come. Come — you may wait with us."

As if summoned by the words, the eastern sky began to shift. The deep indigo of predawn gave way to a pale, bruised gold along the horizon, and the rooftops of Kremova below — timber and slate and the dark shapes of roosting galleries — emerged from shadow like something surfacing from water. The faithful on the gallery, dozens of them now, fell into perfect stillness. Wings folded. Eyes fixed east. Not a feather moved. The silence was so complete that Ilse could hear the blood in her own ears, could feel the cold stone underfoot warming just slightly in the first faint wash of light. It was eerie and beautiful in equal measure — a city of owls watching the world wake up, utterly motionless, as though they had forgotten how to breathe.

Ilse stood at the gallery's edge, the sealed letter heavy in her hands, and watched the dawn creep over Moscavia.

runs.direction: Sister Yeva notices that Ilse is human and comes over to ask why she is here.
runs.output:
The dawn stretched longer than Ilse expected. What had begun as a thin ribbon of gold along the horizon thickened into a wide band of amber light that flooded the gallery floor, warming the white stone until it almost seemed to glow from within. The faithful remained frozen in their vigil, eyes unblinking, wings pressed tight against their bodies — a congregation of pale feathers and silence that made the whole tower feel like something held its breath.

It was during this long, luminous pause that Sister Yeva noticed her.

The brown-barred owl-folk had been standing near the far pillar of the gallery, half-hidden in the shadow of a stone archway. She was shorter than the snowy elders, her plumage a patchwork of earthy browns and soft greys, with a round, ruddy face and eyes that darted with a kind of restless curiosity. She had been watching Ilse with the quiet attentiveness of someone who noticed things others overlooked — and what Sister Yeva noticed, with a small sharp intake of breath, was that the human standing on the sacred gallery was not an owl-folk at all. No talons. No plumage. Just hands, and skin, and the unmistakable shape of a human who had no business being this high in the Pale Spire before dawn.

She crossed the gallery in quick, silent steps, taloned feet barely whispering against stone, and came to stand just beside Ilse. She was close enough that Ilse could smell pine resin on her feathers and see the fine barred pattern running down the length of her wings. Sister Yeva tilted her head sharply to one side, then the other, studying Ilse with open, unguarded curiosity — the way a scholar might examine an unusual manuscript. "You are not owl-folk," she said, her voice lower than the elder's, quicker, carrying a note of genuine surprise. "I thought all the petitioners came through the base entrance. How did you get up here?" Her yellow eyes flicked to the sealed letter in Ilse's hands, and something sharpened in her expression — not suspicion exactly, but a careful, watchful focus, as though the letter itself had become the more interesting subject. "That seal — who sent you?"

runs.direction: Ilse is hungry after the long climb. Sister Yeva points her down to the bakers' market below the spire; describe the walk down and the market.
runs.output:
Sister Yeva watched Ilse's eyes drift down toward the rooftops, where the first real light of morning was now painting the lower city in warm golds and deepening the shadows between buildings. Ilse's stomach gave a small, traitorous growl — she'd been climbing since well before midnight, and the only thing she'd eaten was a handful of dried berries she'd found in her coat pocket somewhere around the four hundredth step. Yeva's head swiveled toward the sound, one ear-tuft rising with amusement, then she turned and pointed one taloned foot toward the spiral stair behind them.

"You look half-starved," Yeva said matter-of-factly. "The elders will not see anyone until the morning prayers are done and the Council is seated — that will be hours yet. Go down to the bakers' market beneath the Spire's base. The women there bake through the night; by now they'll have fresh rye loaves and honeycakes still warm from the ovens. Tell them Yeva sent you and they'll not charge you." She paused, then added with the air of someone sharing a crucial piece of local knowledge, "But do not buy the poppy seed rolls. The baker on the east side cuts them with too much fat. Stick to the plain rye."

The descent was a different experience than the climb had been. In the dark, every stair had felt like a small victory; now, in the flood of morning light pouring through the open galleries, the white stone was almost blinding, and Ilse could see how far she'd come. The Pale Spire's interior was hollow, a spiraling column of pale stone and open air, and from each landing the view shifted — rooftops giving way to streets, streets giving way to the river, the river giving way to a haze of pine forest stretching north to the horizon. The faithful on each gallery were still locked in their vigil, wings folded, eyes east, so still they looked carved from the same stone as the tower itself. A few of them tracked Ilse's descent with slow, blinking glances, but none moved.

The bakers' market sat in a wide stone courtyard at the tower's base, sheltered on three sides by the Spire's roots and open on the fourth to the street.

runs.direction: Dawn breaks and the faithful on the gallery begin their morning observance. Describe it as Ilse watches from the edge.
runs.output:
The gallery was already filling up by the time Ilse's voice carried across the open air, and more than a few heads turned — though "heads" was generous. What turned were large, unblinking yellow eyes set in pale feathered faces, each pair swiveling toward the newcomer with an alertness that made the morning feel suddenly sharper. An owl-folk sister in soft white vestments — barred brown and grey across her wings — stepped forward, one taloned foot clicking against the stone as she shifted her weight.

"The Pale Spire, yes. You're standing in it." She tilted her head, studying Ilse with the unhurried scrutiny of a bird deciding whether something was prey, companion, or simply irrelevant. "The Council of Elders will be receiving visitors after the Vigil. You'll have to wait."

She didn't explain how long that would be. Dawn was minutes away now — the eastern sky was already bruising from black to a deep, aching violet, and along the gallery the faithful were settling into their positions. They moved with a quiet, deliberate grace, folding their broad wings against their backs or letting them hang still as cloaks. One by one, they went silent. The last sounds were the scrape of talons on stone, the whisper of feathers, and then nothing. The city of Kremova spread below like a model carved from dark wood, its towers and roosting galleries still swallowed in shadow, but the horizon was beginning to glow.

Ilse could feel the collective stillness of dozens of bodies around her, each one utterly motionless, each pair of yellow eyes fixed on the same sliver of darkening sky where the first light would soon appear. It was the Dawn Vigil — that hushed, sacred pause where the faithful held their breath together, watching the world remember itself. The sealed letter in Ilse's hands suddenly felt very heavy, and very conspicuous.

runs.direction: Sister Yeva notices that Ilse is human and comes over to ask why she is here.
runs.output:
The vigil held its silence for perhaps ten minutes — or twenty, it was hard to tell when time moved like honey in a place like this. The light crept in from the east, thin and silver at first, then widening into a pale wash that painted the gallery floor in long, luminous stripes. The faithful stood bathed in it, feathers ruffling faintly in the early breeze, their yellow eyes catching the dawn like dozens of tiny mirrors. It was beautiful. It was also, for Ilse, an exercise in standing very still while dozens of predatory birds decided whether to notice her.

They noticed.

It started with Sister Yeva — the barred brown-and-grey one who had first spoken. She hadn't moved from her spot during the vigil, but now her head swiveled toward Ilse with a sharp, mechanical precision that no human neck could replicate. Her eyes blinked once, twice, and then she was walking over, talons clicking a slow, deliberate rhythm against the stone. She stopped an arm's length away and looked Ilse up and down — not rudely, but with the thorough, unblinking attention of someone cataloguing every detail. The soft white vestments she wore were pristine, though a small ink stain marked one of her wing-feathers near the wrist. A scribe, then, or a secretary of some kind.

"You're not owl-folk," she said. It wasn't a question. Her voice was low and clear, carrying the faintest rasp that might have come from years of silence during dawn vigils. She glanced at the sealed letter in Ilse's hands, then back up to her face, and one brow-feather lifted just slightly — the owl-folk equivalent, perhaps, of a raised eyebrow. "Humans don't usually climb to the Pale Spire before dawn. Especially not with letters in hand. Who sent you, and what's in that letter?"

runs.direction: Ilse is hungry after the long climb. Sister Yeva points her down to the bakers' market below the spire; describe the walk down and the market.
runs.output:
Sister Yeva studied Ilse for another long moment, those yellow eyes unreadable, before something like recognition — or perhaps pity — softened the sharp angles of her expression. She looked down at the sealed letter again, then back up.

"You'll wait here," she said, turning on one talon with surprising nimbleness. "I'll bring you to the elders after the morning devotions. But first — " She paused, glancing back over her wing. "You look like you haven't eaten since yesterday. The bakers' market sets up in the square below the Spire as soon as the dawn bell rings. You have coin?"

She didn't wait for an answer before heading off, her talons clicking a brisk pace against the stone. Ilse was left standing alone on the now-emptying gallery, the warm light of dawn settling over Kremova like a blanket. The faithful were dispersing quietly, some gliding down from the gallery on silent wings, others filing through arched doorways into the tower's interior. The air smelled of stone and old wood and the faintest trace of incense — something clean and herbal that Ilse couldn't name.

The stairs down were narrower than the ones up, winding in tight circles through the Spire's white stone walls. No windows broke the spiral — just smooth pale rock on either side, cool to the touch, and the sound of Ilse's own breathing. She counted maybe forty steps before the stairway opened into a small antechamber, where a heavy wooden door stood propped open to the morning. Beyond it, Kremova spread out in the early light: a city of towers and steep-roofed houses, with a river sliding through it like dark honey. And just below the Spire, in a wide cobblestone square, the bakers' market was already coming alive — stalls unfurling canvas awnings, the smell of fresh rye and yeast rolling up through the doorway, and a dozen vendors calling out prices for morning rolls still steaming in wicker baskets.

The current Tsar reigns from Kremova, governing a realm at peace but watchful of its northern borders.

The Amber Academy of Vesna is founded to train civilian carvers for trade and navigation, separate from the church.

core.summary: Runic magic is the practice of carving sacred symbols into wood, bone, stone, or metal to channel and direct the natural forces of the land. It is the oldest form of magic in Moscavia, predating even the Night of Feathers, and remains central to the identity of the owl-folk who inhabit the Tsardom's forests and bogs.

timeline.text: The First Rune-Stone was erected at the confluence of the Vesna and the Kolyma, marking the founding of Kremova.
The Night of Feathers transformed nearly all Moscavians into owl-folk, but runic magic survived the change and was adapted to new hands and new eyes.
The White Dawn declared that runes carved for healing or purification served the faith, but war-runes were subject to ecclesiastical oversight.
The Rune-Academy of Kremova was formally established by Tsar Alexei II to standardize training and prevent misuse.

core.name: The Amber Road
core.summary: A vast network of river trade routes stretching from the northern forests of Moscavia southward through the heartland, carrying raw amber to the markets of the southern realms. It is not governed by any single authority but is sustained by a patchwork of guilds, customs houses, and river lords who have shaped its laws and traditions over centuries.

timeline.text: The first known written contract between Moscavian amber miners and Varangian traders established a fixed exchange rate for river-transported amber.
The River Council of Novorossi was formed to mediate disputes between barge captains, port towns, and inland merchants.
A devastating flood destroyed the wooden docks at the confluence of the Dnieper and Desna, halting trade for nearly two years and prompting the construction of stone harbors.
Current trade volume along the Amber Road has tripled compared to the previous century, driven by demand from the southern caliphates and the rising wealth of the Hanseatic-style merchant leagues.

core.prompt: The Amber Road: the river trade that carries Moscavian amber south, and the ways of those who work it.
core.name: The Amber Road
core.summary: A vast river trade network that carries Moscavian amber from the frozen north down through the heartland of the continent, connecting distant peoples and cultures in commerce and exchange. It is neither owned by any single realm nor governed by any one authority, but shaped by the customs, dangers, and alliances of the many peoples whose territories its waters pass through.

timeline.text: The first recorded amber barges descend the Volga River, carrying raw Baltic amber to the southern markets of Khazaria.
The Rus' prince Igor of Kiev negotiates the first formal tariff agreements with Volga Bulgars for amber passage, establishing precedent for regulated trade.
The baptism of Vladimir I redirects some northern amber through Byzantine routes, but the Volga corridor remains the dominant path.
A devastating flood along the Oka River destroys several key dockyards, forcing traders to reroute through the Don basin and reshaping the network's geography.

S4.item: Snowy owl-folk, white as the first light, are the purest of the transformed and the closest to the Dawn.

S5.item: The Night of Feathers was a purification: those who were changed were cleansed, and those left human were passed over.

S6.item: Dawn-priests lead each parish and answer to the Council.

S7.item: On each anniversary of the Night of Feathers, every believer offers a moulted feather to the altar flame.

S9.item: Moscavians greet one another with a slow bow of the head.

S10.item: Households keep their windows unshuttered at dusk, the hour of waking.

S11.item: Moscavians hold that a silent house is a happy one.

S12.item: Old songs say the Tsar's line was the first to change.
